en: Preface to the Compendium of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra:
Ah, how vast this Way is! It cannot be contained within sounds. At Vulture Peak, the Dharma was transmitted through a smile; at Shaolin, the meaning was silently revealed by facing a wall.

It was solely the transmission of the essential heart-mind, established without words or texts, so that those who encounter it may find mutual resonance within their very brows and foreheads. Great indeed!
The Way is without remainder; yet, without the application of needles or moxibustion, chronic ailments are suddenly dispelled.

Alas, how is it that students cling to the karmic habits of the past and are tossed by the winds and waves of their own views? There are those for whom the *āmra* fruit gradually ripens, but those upon whom the sun’s orb suddenly shines are few.
When the lunar miasma appears alongside [the light], gold ore and dross become intermingled; thus, the wondrous luminosity is frequently obscured by dust and grime.

How much more so when, as time passes, transmission inevitably becomes erroneous; and as teachers multiply, practice inevitably becomes corrupt. Without these teachings recorded in books, how could they be shown as proof?
Thereupon, my ancestors came from the West and pointed out these secret texts, transmitting them together with their instructions.

This was intended so that even as generations change, the Dharma would remain ever more firm; and even as individuals may err, the texts would still survive. For one who merely has the will to sift through the sand, what further need is there?
It is difficult to obtain such a treasure. My ancestor Bodhidharma once said: "I possess four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which is the heart-seal of all Buddhas.
I entrust it to the Second Patriarch, charging him to protect and uphold it, and transmit it to future masters.

It has been praised through successive generations as taking those who are vessels for the Mahāyāna and bestowing upon them the precious essence of the supreme flavor; it cleanses even the most subtle transgressions and establishes one in that state of true purity.

It is simply because India is a distant land and its literary language differs in pronunciation; thus, readers spend ten days merely struggling with the punctuation and word division, let alone being able to examine the text to perceive its meaning and clearly grasp it within their own hearts and minds.
I deeply lament that the wondrous intent of the Buddha-King has been neglected and allowed to perish along with the bookworms.
Reflecting on this, I imagine the hearts of the various sages must be chilled with sorrow; how could a benevolent person sit idly by and watch this? I have previously...
Through this sincere devotion and yearning, the profound meaning was secretly communicated. Continuing my studies by the light of the lamp, the Great Principle became clearly manifest.

I sighed deeply that previous texts were so archaic and obscure that they caused later students to abandon their study; therefore, I compiled and arranged the essential pivot of the mysteries and composed a commentary upon them.

Just as I was about to open the secret scriptures from the lapis lazuli case and apply myself to the task on an auspicious day, a woman adorned in gold appeared in a dream at midnight and said: "Force..."

I, [Your Servant], am not quick-witted; yet, through the grace of the humble praise, both [the commentary and the verses] have been completed. I hope that fellow students may ascend this path so that they may observe with their eyes and realize with their minds.

After a period of one year, these four fascicles have already been finished. I do not dare to circulate them alongside the authentic scriptures, but shall instead title them the *Lengqie jing zuan* (Compendium of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra).

Thus, the meanings of the one hundred and eight phrases have been arranged into over seventy sections, capturing the profound essence of those mysteries and establishing headings accordingly, so that students may...
By examining the texts one attains their meaning, and by means of that meaning one verifies the mind. This is not merely for the sake of transmitting what has been certified by the Buddha;

it is also to ensure that these magnificent writings do not fall into ruin. Alas! Sentient beings are shrouded in darkness and entangled by habitual karma. Unaware that they are casting away their own family wealth, they spend their days hauling dung for others.

Their natures and consciousnesses are fickle and fleeting as they rush toward old age and death, even sinking into the four modes of birth and circling through the six realms of existence. In the midst of this—

There are those of the Supreme Vehicle who find it difficult to escape the dust of extreme views. Those who obliterate mental characteristics within the emptiness of annihilation do not realize they are instead drowning in non-existence;

those who identify with the illusory dust of the spiritual consciousness do not realize they are instead falling into existence. How could the Great Way of Non-action ever fall into the dust of consciousness?
To deliberate upon it is to lose the source; to clarify the spirit only serves to stir it further. When the numinous light continues in succession, its reflections...

Concealing the body within, sit in silence and contemplate emptiness; this is the livelihood within the cave. How much more so regarding seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing—how could these be recognized as True Suchness?
Why then take words and language to be the Master’s secret intent? Once the spiritual source has returned to its root, what need is there to worry that all phenomena are not true?
Therefore, our Great Benevolent One extensively bestowed skillful means to reveal the mystery of the one mind and to block off various views.

[This is] heterodox. If you must surely desire to draw the pure essence of the *tīrtha* (clarified butter) to universally drench the impoverished sons, then employ supramundane wisdom to enter the minds of ordinary beings;
point out their flaws and polish away their defilements. Forge the true mind through the seven natures and seven meanings;
eliminate emotional consciousness through the three marks and four *dhyānas*. Establish the four minor fruits to dispel empty conceptions; recount the five *anantarya* [sins] to eradicate delusion.

Because the realization attained through conditions was not yet perfected, the ten stages (*bhūmi*) were established; because the signlessness of all phenomena was investigated, the seven emptinesses were revealed.
Through the three wisdoms and three bodies, one is led to return together to the *dharmakāya*; through the two dharmas and five dharmas, one is led to reach the same foundation as the *tathatā*.
This is solely because the mind clings to the measure of views; who would have known that the error lay in a mere fraction? Therefore, the state beyond conceptualization is shown.

The *hunpan* (mixed-intrusion) then reveals the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) of non-self; it severs the threads of delusion so they do not continue, enabling one to wear the Precious Seal of True Emptiness.
It extinguishes existence and non-existence, transcends both nature and non-nature, and awakens the mind for the sake of future generations.
Severing the views of emotional attachment, one opens the field of self-awakening. It is hoped that the ore-stones will be entirely discarded, so that true gold may permeate the entire body.
Thus, one blocks the divergent paths ahead of the station and inspects the scars upon the ground;

scraping away the dust that obscures the gold and penetrating the veils of the membrane, one causes the two hindrances to be suddenly exhausted. With no vehicle left to ascend, one is forever liberated from birth after birth.

Like a soiled garment, one sits and advances toward the wondrous stage of suchness (*tathatā*). For this reason, the Precious Treasury hangs its banner, yet alone designates it as the "Mind Section" (*citta-pada*);
the region west of the Yangtze River offers praise, yet once sighed that it is "Gateless," also calling it the "Mind Section. To call it the "Mind Section" means there is no school outside the mind;
to call it "Gateless" means that having gates is a departure from the Dharma. Looking up to this wondrous purport, there is indeed a true refuge where precious treasures are arrayed in profusion.

One seeks only the great price; medical prescriptions are manifold and complex, yet they are applied only for minor ailments. Once the great price is obtained, all other goods may be discarded; once the minor ailment is eliminated, what use are the various prescriptions?
The transmission between the Buddhas of the past consists solely of this One Mind. The secret scripture of the *Ghanavyūha* (Dense Array) removes only the disease of the mind.
True consciousness is empty and quiescent; through false emotions, conditions arise. When one returns to the source of emptiness and quiescence, the dust of emotional afflictions naturally vanishes.

This very true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*) is vast and without dependence; subject and object are both forgotten, and the continuity of conditions is forever severed. This is called right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*). How could there be anything else to seek?
To find the original pearl is nothing other than retrieving an old possession from within one's own home; to remove the cataract from the eye means that flowers naturally no longer appear in the sky.
Water does not possess a separate essence, yet it freely forms waves; the mirror has no mind of its own—how could this be an obstacle?
Illuminating all things, it reveals the Buddha’s secret intent; a thousand sages return to this same path. Though paper and brush may exhaust themselves, praise can never reach its end.
This is why I, a fool, do not decline to offer the light of a torch to assist the radiance of the sun. I universally pray that all sentient beings may dwell together in the state beyond outflows.
Preface by Yang Yanguo, a resident of Taibao.

Chapter One: The Heart of All Buddha-Speech.
The five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness—when these are thoroughly and ultimately realized, they are termed the five dharmas:
namely, name, appearance, conceptualization, correct knowledge, and suchness. Conceptualization, dependent origination, and the perfected nature are termed the three natures.
The three natures, consciousness—which refers to the eight consciousnesses—and the two kinds of selflessness—which refer to the self and phenomena—are the core of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
It takes the Buddha’s mind-essence as its primary tenet and has no fixed gate as its dharma-gate; thus, its establishment depends upon these.
The mind of all Buddhas is supreme.
This mind is like the solid heartwood of a tree; it is not a mind of discursive thought.
It is the phrase "constant," yet it is not a phrase of constancy.
There are three kinds of "constant" (cháng). This "constant" differs from the previous "constant" in its Sanskrit pronunciation.
"Numerical phrases" and "non-numerical phrases" refer to the enumeration of these things.
"Numerical phrases and non-numerical phrases—this enumeration, O Mahāmati, consists of one hundred and eight phrases.
These were spoken by the Buddhas of the past; you and the other bodhisattvas should practice and study them."
Chapter One: Clarifying the True Reality.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing are there for the various consciousnesses?"
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "All consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing. These are not to be known through discursive thought;
only the wisdom of *prajñā* can illuminate and contemplate them."
The various consciousnesses have two modes of arising:
namely, arising as a continuous flow, and arising through the conditions of mental attention. This is like the flowing of water and the manifestation of its forms.
It arises from perceiving all forms and characteristics. It has two modes of abiding:
the abiding of the stream and the abiding of characteristics. It has two modes of cessation: the cessation of the stream and the cessation of characteristics.
Mahāmati, the various consciousnesses have three kinds of characteristics: the characteristic of transformation, the characteristic of activity, and the characteristic of reality.
The "true aspect" (*xiang*) refers to the eternally abiding true mind. This is what is meant in the following passage: "In its true aspect, it is truly not extinguished.
The "karmic aspect" (*ye xiang*) means that the true aspect is shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*), and karma arises therefrom; hence it is called the karmic aspect.

The "transformative aspect" (*zhuan xiang*) means that because it is shrouded by ignorance, that which was originally unmoving now undergoes transformation and becomes defiled; hence it is called transformative.
Characteristics.
Mahāmati, briefly stated there are three kinds of consciousness; in detail, there are eight characteristics.
These eight characteristics are the eight consciousnesses.

What are these three? They are the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*), and the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vikaṭpa-vastu-vijñāna*).

Because it is like suchness (*tathatā*) and its true mark, utterly transcending dust and delusion, it is called the "true consciousness. Because it is able to receive the forms that are manifested, it is called the "manifesting consciousness";
this is the eighth consciousness of the various sūtras, also termed the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālaya-vijñāna*). Form is the object...
The "manifesting consciousness" (xiànshí) is that which manifests; because it manifests objects like a mirror reflects images, it is called the manifesting consciousness.
The "consciousness that discriminates phenomena" (fēnbié shìshí) refers to the sixth mental consciousness (manovijñāna) mentioned in various sūtras.
Just as a clear mirror holds all forms and images, so too does the manifesting consciousness appear in its locus.

This manifesting consciousness and the discerning consciousness of objects—these two have characteristics of being perishable and imperishable, respectively, and they serve as mutual causes for one another.

That which perishes is the discriminating consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*). This means that once discrimination has occurred, it then perishes. That which does not perish is the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*).

This means that although what is manifested may cease, that which is capable of manifesting it remains eternally present. Because these two are mutually dependent, they are called "successive causes" (*pāramparyahetu*).

The inconceivable perfuming and the inconceivable transformation are the causes of the manifesting consciousness (*ādarśa-vijñāna*). The grasping of various objects and the perfuming of beginningless false discrimination are the causes of the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*viṣaya-vikalpa-vijñāna*).

Originally, there were no characteristics of the various consciousnesses. Due to the beginningless, subtle permeation and various transformations, the manifesting consciousness (ādarśa-vijñāna) arises.
Because it grasps at all sensory objects and is permeated by false conceptualization, the consciousness of discerning phenomena (pravṛtti-vijñāna) arises.
Mahāmati, if that true consciousness is covered and the various unrealities and false imaginings are extinguished, then all the sense-faculties and consciousnesses are extinguished;
this is called the extinction of characteristics.
The term "covering" (*āvaraṇa*) also carries the sense of "reversal. This refers to turning the light back upon itself and reflecting inward to return to true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*).
When all faculties and objects (*indriya-viṣaya*) thus dissolve into the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), how could any inherent nature or characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) possibly be perceived?
Mahāmati, as for the cessation of continuity: when the cause of continuity ceases, then continuity ceases; when that from which it proceeds and its objective support cease, then continuity ceases.
Why is this? Because these are its basis. "Basis" refers to the habitual perfuming of beginningless false discrimination.
"Objective support" refers to the false discrimination regarding the objects of consciousness, such as the manifestations of one's own mind.

The source from which [consciousness] arises, its objects of perception, and its supports are all causes for the continuity of illusory appearances. Only by extinguishing these causes will the continuity cease.
The true nature of the single mind is fundamentally vast and empty; it is utterly detached from the sense organs and their objects—what further support could it possibly have?
The mind is not of itself the mind; what, then, could it take as an object? It is merely because one is stuck in habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that one has not yet escaped dependence on others.
Although one may have awakened to the original mind and attained clarity, if the conditions for the arising of mental characteristics remain, delusion will not cease.

Only when this continuity of illness is entirely eliminated does one enter the wondrous ground of suchness (*tathatā*). That the Tathāgata’s continuity has ceased is precisely for this reason. To insistently establish a "self" [is the error].
The mind is identical to the objects of consciousness; therefore, it is called "delusive discrimination regarding objects equal to consciousness.
Mahāmati, it is like a lump of clay or fine dust (and so forth, until: yet its own true characteristic is in fact never extinguished.
Because of true reality (*tathatā*), there is the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); because of the storehouse consciousness, there are the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
Since they have a cause, they are not different [from it]. If true reality does not perish, then the storehouse consciousness also does not perish.

As for the evolving consciousnesses, that which is grasped by them is what is called the "aspect of karma" (*karmalakṣaṇa*). This has never failed to perish. That one perishes while the other does not perish means they are not [identical].
They are not different. That which is not different is its essence (*tattva*); that which is different is its function (*vṛtti*).

For example, although a lump of clay and a golden vessel are not identical, they are both fundamentally derived from fine dust and gold, respectively. This illustrates that although the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) associated with karmic characteristics may cease, they all fundamentally derive from the unceasing true nature (*dharmatā*).
Therefore, Mahāmati, it is not that consciousness perishes through its own intrinsic characteristics. (And so forth... The beginningless stream must be severed.
Only when the beginningless stream is severed is the view [of self] severed; for one has failed to realize that all is mind-only.
Mahāmati, non-Buddhists speak of a causal source for the continuous flow [of existence] (up to: whether it be time or atoms).
They claim this is a distinct cause of the non-Buddhists, and that it is not necessarily produced from the realm of the eye, the realm of consciousness, the realm of form, and the realm of ignorance.
Furthermore, there is a discourse based on the "Excellence" (Śrī-mālā) Sūtra. The Treatise states: "The true nature does not perish; this is the 'One Mind' transmitted by the Dharma.
It is luminous, spiritual, and profoundly penetrating, spanning from antiquity to the present. When its source is investigated, it is found to be without interval or admixture.

Through the conjunction with deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*), the various consciousnesses arise. From what these various consciousnesses manifest, the various phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) arise. These various phenomena...
It is not permanent; rather, there is arising, abiding, and ceasing. To awaken to this is the bliss of *nirvāṇa*; to be deluded by it is the river of birth and death.
One who has attained the Way awakens to the fact that these manifested illusory objects are unreal, all being permeated by beginningless false conceptualization.

By turning the light back upon itself and reflecting inward, one returns to true consciousness. It is like water returning to its source in a pit, where its wandering currents naturally cease; it is like fire...

Returning to emptiness, the radiance suddenly vanishes; one may then be carefree and self-sovereign, with both mind and objects forgotten, forever dismissing all sensory dusts and abiding steadfastly in the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Yet, because habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) still remain, one cannot avoid clinging to conditions and remains dependent on others throughout the day.
Failing to recognize this for oneself, one forcibly gives rise to intellectual views and establishes them as one's own fundamental mind.

Unaware of the aggregates, elements, and storehouse consciousness, one vainly seeks the Buddha by means of the Buddha—on one hand relying on external objects, and on the other using the mind to contemplate the mind.

The two illnesses have not yet been eliminated, and delusive appearances continue in succession. Therefore, the Tathāgata necessarily desires that both the objects of perception and the perceiving subject be stilled, that both the conditions and the causes be discarded, that karma be transformed and simultaneously transcended, so that the true mark is eternally pure. This is the Way. It is not obtained from another; it is simply one’s own treasure.

It is vividly manifest before one’s eyes as a solitary luminosity. If you recognize it, you will remain buried in delusion as before. There is no need for acceptance or rejection; it is the original [nature].

It is spontaneously perfected; it is simply the removal of delusive conditions, which is itself the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). The "Chapter on the Essence of the Buddha’s Words" clarifies this alone.
The verse says:
How have we sunk in birth and death throughout kalpas? It is solely because of the causes of consciousness from the past.
One should realize that the two births have no separate essence; one must know that even the eight phases are not external objects.
Sentient beings must believe that [all] arises from mind alone; discrimination is entirely conditioned by the熏 (perfuming) of false imaginings.
If the faculties and objects are both subverted and unreal, then within this, the unextinguished phase returns to the True.
Chapter Two: Discerning Delusion and Illuminating Reality.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of self-nature (svabhāva), up to the mind of the ultimate reality of self-nature.
This is the Sanskrit term *hṛdaya*, which means the core of a tree; it is not the mind of discursive thought.
The mind of discursive thought is the Sanskrit term *citta*.
By means of the mind of the ultimate reality of the self-nature of essence (up to: it does not share in the evil views of the treatises of the non-Buddhists.
To gather various objects and accumulate them within the mind is called "accumulation" (*cita*). That the mind arises and thus the nature arises is called "nature" (*svabhāva*).

That the nature arises and its characteristics manifest is called "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). That the four great elements follow from this is called "great elements" (*mahābhūta*). That which arises in dependence on others is called "cause" (*hetu*); [it is] the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

That which acts is called "conditions" (*pratyaya*). That which is the perfect illumination of the awakened nature is called "accomplishment. Within the true aspect of suchness (*tathatā*), no other conditions can enter.

It is only through deluded sentiment that illusions arise and various natures are produced. It is solely by means of great awakening’s illuminating contemplation of the true source that one realizes those produced natures are nothing but false manifestations.
Those various entities are quiescent and fundamentally empty; they are all the self-manifesting direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the awakened mind. Thus one knows.
Once [the self] has manifested, the illusory dust is extinguished; when illusion is extinguished, awakening is perfected, which is precisely suchness as it is.
The self-nature of the *Laṅkāvatāra* is entirely like this. Because the light of the Way reflects back upon the one mind, it is called "mind" (*citta*).

Because clarifying the mind must be rooted in the wisdom that illuminates the heterodox, it is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*). Because employing wisdom must value the discernment of decisive judgment, it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*). There is...
Only after wisdom does right view become clear; therefore, it is called "view. Only when one possesses right view can one transcend existence and non-existence;
therefore, it is called "transcending the two views. Having transcended the two views, one then transcends the stage of the Buddha’s son; therefore, it is called the "son's stage.
Once the son's stage has been transcended, one then relinquishes the consecration of the Cloud of Dharma and ascends to the site of perfect enlightenment; therefore, it is called "thus."
Come! Since arriving at the Tathāgata, one employs the supramundane mind to create this realm, transcending all mundane dust and delusion and surpassing all heterodox schools.
Externalists cannot even tread upon its threshold, and those of the Two Vehicles cannot penetrate its depths;

therefore, it is called the "Ultimate Truth" (paramārtha). Now, the single mind is fundamentally quiescent; how could there be such things as essence or characteristics? All phenomena are empty; who then can name them a "realm"?
However, the Tathāgata’s words differ in their intrinsic nature. All [teachings] use consciousness to refute external objects; thus it is said that the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is not uniform.
This is because all [teachings] transcend [duality] and are entirely true. It is precisely because external objects do not defile it that it alone is entirely true.
The Tathāgata’s accomplishment of the mental dharmas truly arises from this; therefore, it is called the "ultimate mind" (*paramārtha-citta*).
How could it be shared with the evil views of the non-Buddhist treatises? That is to say, it is not the false conceptualization and views regarding one's own sphere of experience.
The evil views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) give rise only to views of false conceptualization within their own domain;

they do not realize that these are manifestations of their own minds. (And so forth... I shall now explain how they perceive the illusory objects manifested by their own minds according to their respective views.

Because the suffering of the three realms of existence has been extinguished, one is able to perceive that which is manifested by one's own mind; regarding these manifested objects, they suddenly appear like illusions or transformations.
Mahāmati, if there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas...
From those below the level of śramaṇas up to those who falsely claim to speak with omniscience, all hold the views of external paths;

such are their faults (and so forth). The Buddha told Mahāmati: "To speak of non-existence refers to things such as rabbit horns or tortoise hair;
these are expressions currently used in the world."
That which does not exist yet appears to exist is merely worldly discourse.
Mahāmati, it is neither an intrinsic nature nor a lack of intrinsic nature; it is simply verbal expression.
The Buddha told him that verbal expression does not possess an intrinsic nature, nor is it both existent and non-existent by nature.
As you have said, one cannot know [reality] as it truly is within the house of the three realms of saṃsāra.
The verse says:
Do not hold that causes and conditions arise from another; Cease all discourse regarding whether their nature exists or does not exist.
If one realizes that it is only mind, or that the manifested objects are like the clarity of a mirror or the resonance of a bell, they are as they truly are (tathatā).

This is the twenty-ninth section on being free from the confusion of dualistic perception. (Delusion consists of false conceptualization; who would not agree? Ordinary people are deluded regarding awakening and ignorance, remaining in darkness without self-awareness.)

The two vehicles perceive delusion as inversion; they are mired in ignorance and unaware of it themselves. Like one who has an illness but refuses to take medicine, they mistake inversion for reality, and by taking such "medicine," they only increase their afflictions.

Consequently, the true permanence can find no way to be restored. Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of permanence for those who are confused and deluded. The Patriarch said: "Delusion gives rise to the confusion of stillness;
awakening is free from likes and dislikes. At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding the term 'permanence,' what does it refer to?"
Regarding those who claim that sound is eternal: on what basis do they say so?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is because of delusion (*bhrānti*).
By clinging to delusion, one takes it to be a perversion, and thus the mind of arising and ceasing arises. This is why one is bound by grasping."
If one abandons [the world] yet does not attain the eternal, the Patriarch said: "It is precisely because of grasping and abandoning that one is thus inferior.
Therefore, when Mahāmati asked about the eternal, the Buddha replied that it is a delusive confusion.
Because of that delusion, even the noble ones appear [as such], yet they are not inverted;
the noble ones also manifest delusion in common with ordinary people. However, their non-inversion and inversion differ from those of ordinary people in terms of their conceptualization.
This is not true wisdom. Yet it is not that they do not manifest;
to say they do is called wisdom. They are not like wood or stone—how could they fail to manifest? They are merely like illusions; though they manifest, they do not manifest.
Why is this? It is because it is free from both existence and non-existence.
From the very beginning, it is free from existence; it arises due to delusion. When a single film obscures the eye, illusory flowers fall in confusion.
How could that [emptiness] possibly give rise to impermanence?
What is the delusion that is free from existence and non-existence? It refers to the various objective spheres of all foolish commoners.
These various objective spheres are, for example, like the unadorned Ganges River.
Just as with that Ganges River, because hungry ghosts see it or do not see it, it lacks the nature of being a delusive confusion.
For the hungry ghosts, the fact that they do not see water in the river does not mean the Ganges lacks its own nature.
Likewise, those foolish people are submerged in delusive confusion and do not realize it themselves.
Because it appears as something else, it is not non-existent;
for others who possess cognitive awareness perceive it as the Ganges, and thus it possesses the nature of being the Ganges.
Just as those śrāvakas grasp it as truly existent, one should cause that nature of delusive appearance to be destroyed.
Such is delusion. For the noble ones, there is neither inversion nor non-inversion; therefore, delusion is eternal, because its characteristics are not destroyed.
Regarding this delusion, it is not that the noble ones possess the nature of non-delusion while ordinary fools do not, such that they fail to recognize it themselves; nor is it...
Just as the two vehicles possess a nature of delusion and strive to destroy it, they depart from both inverted and non-inverted awareness;

thus, without anticipating permanence, they become permanent of their own accord. The reason they are permanent is that they have never perceived characteristics as such and have striven to extinguish them.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states: [and so forth].
Mahāmati, what is the reality of delusion? (And so forth... Within this delusion, there is not even the slightest notion that constitutes the objective characteristics of noble wisdom.
For the noble ones, regarding this delusion, both the perception of it as illusory and the perception of it as non-illusory are entirely absent; having transcended these, [they abide in reality].

Externally, there is a slight degree of cognition, which is precisely the cognition of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Therefore, it is said that this is not the characteristic of the object of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
Mahāmati, whatever exists is the false discourse of fools; it is not the discourse of the noble ones.
"Existence" refers to the grasping at the nature of delusion as being existent; this is merely foolish and false.
That delusion consists of inverted and non-inverted conceptualizations, which give rise to two kinds of natures.
Although those below possess the lineage of the noble ones, they still harbor non-perverted false conceptualizations.

Mahāmati, from that very same delusive confusion, false conceptualizations give rise to the lineage of the Pratyekabuddhayāna; this refers to not closely adhering to the specific and general characteristics of that very delusion.
There is awakening through conditions; it is not that there is no conceptual attachment. Rather, there is that which is awakened to, yet one does not cling to it.

How is it that a wise person gives rise to the lineage of the Buddha-vehicle from within that very delusion? It is by awakening to the fact that all is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, and that external natures have no inherent reality, being free from the marks of false conceptualization.
This means that one does not give rise to the notion of non-existence regarding external phenomena;
rather, one gives rise to the lineage of the Buddha-vehicle. This is called the arising of the lineage of the Buddha-vehicle from within that very delusion.

Although it is called the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*), because it involves the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*), it cannot escape delusive thought (*vikalpa*). If one knows it to be like an illusion, then even the Buddha-vehicle is likewise delusive.
Furthermore, the nature of various phenomena is the deluded conception of ordinary beings, which gives rise to the lineage of the foolish.
Foolish people discriminate among the natures of various phenomena, determining them to be thus and not otherwise; therefore, this is called "delusive conceptualization.
These are neither existent things nor non-existent things; this is what is meant by the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*).
Whether they be noble ones or ordinary people, all who perceive sounds through conditions do so within delusion, yet from this arise their respective spiritual capacities (*gotra*).

Within those capacities, the various phenomena are neither identical to material objects nor are they non-objects; they all manifest in accordance with the mind. Therefore, it is said that this is the meaning of "spiritual capacity."
Mahāmati, that very delusion is non-conceptualization (even unto... Therefore, it is said that "reality (tathatā) is free from the mind.

Because the nature of delusion itself is non-conceptualization, the noble ones (*ārya*) are able to transform and abandon the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the mind, intellect, and consciousness, thereby becoming *tathatā*.
When it is said that reality is free from the mind, it means it is free from the mind, intellect, and consciousness.
[And so forth.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if delusion is like an illusion, it should further act as a cause for other delusions;
that is to say, all things being like illusions, subsequent delusions arise through the successive transformation of preceding ones, and all other delusions arise based upon this. Furthermore—
This is the doubt of Mahāmati.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not a cause of delusion, because it does not give rise to faults. Illusion does not give rise to faults, for it is devoid of false conceptualization."
All things are like illusions; all faults are subtly extinguished. The ability to extinguish these faults arises because there are no delusions.
Mahāmati, an illusion arises from the presence of another [an external cause], not from the locus of the habitual tendencies of the faults of false imagination.
Only through that awakened clarity can one be like a magical illusion;
therefore, no fault arises. Mahāmati, this is the deluded conceptual attachment of foolish people, not that of the noble sages.
Other afflictions act as causes; because of this, doubt arises. This is the calculation of fools, not that of the noble ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:
The Sage does not perceive delusion, nor is there any reality in the interim.
If the interim were truly real, then delusion would be reality itself. Having abandoned all delusions, should any appearance arise, that too is delusion—impurity is like a cataract.
If there is a departure from characteristics, that too is delusion; therefore, it is called "impure. The verse says:
In silent, empty stillness, all calculation ceases; Delusive doubt and confusion ruin the true and constant.
Yet one attempts to dispel inversion with conscious thought, Agitating and destroying the mindless Buddha-dharmadhātu.
Reflections do not refuse to appear from the depths of the pool; Whether beautiful or ugly, how could they ever remain hidden within the mirror?
Knowing that all things are like illusions, The myriad phenomena are as fleeting as flashes of lightning.
Chapter Thirty: The Distinction of Illusory Diversity.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, it is not that there is no resemblance to illusion; rather, one perceives all phenomena as being like an illusion. Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
(omitted) ... "When you say that all phenomena are like an illusion, is this because of an attachment to their distinct characteristics?"

"Various" refers to all characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). "Diverse characteristics" refers to inverted characteristics (*viparyāsa-lakṣaṇa*), which are subject to change and differ from one another, just like magical illusions. This is the doubt of Mahāmati.

"If one is attached to various illusory appearances... (up to: World-Honored One, if there were natures that were not like illusions," said Mahāmati, "since they possess the characteristics of a nature, they would not perish immediately; how then could one be attached to them as being like illusions?"
Why is this so? (And so forth... Various appearances manifest like an illusion.
All forms and characteristics are not caused; yet, even though they have no cause, various appearances nonetheless manifest, being just like an illusion.
Mahāmati, however, all dharmas are unreal and perish as swiftly as lightning; thus they are like illusions.
Because dharmas are unreal and perish as swiftly as lightning, they are said to be like illusions.
For example, like a flash of lightning (and so forth), it is not manifest to the foolish;
yet the foolish cling to it and cannot quickly extinguish their attachment. Therefore it is said:
"In this way, all natures (and so forth) are not the manifestation of forms and signs, yet they are clung to as such."

This means that regarding all natures and characteristics, if one can observe them as being without intrinsic nature and thus like an illusion, one does not become attached to the characteristics of form.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not my teaching that non-arising is like an illusion... (and so forth)... it refers to arising and non-arising."
The essence of nature is empty and quiescent. Whatever arises is entirely like an illusion or a dream; therefore, although there is arising, in reality it has never arisen.
One awakens to the fact that what appears is the manifestation of one's own mind; whether existent or non-existent, external natures or non-natures, there is only the manifestation of non-arising.
One merely perceives that within one's own mind there is both existence and non-existence; external entities and non-entities all appear without being produced.

Mahāmati, it is not that my previous and subsequent teachings contain the fault of contradiction (and so forth), nor do they arise from the conditions of various attachments to one's own false imaginings.

"O Mahāmati, the non-Buddhists claim that all phenomena arise from existence and non-existence; they do not say that they arise from the causal conditions of the attachments of one's own mind’s false imaginings.
Mahāmati, it is not that I [teach] that things arise from existence or non-existence... [omitted] ...it is for the purpose of encompassing birth and death."
The statement that humans possess a nature (*prakṛti*) is intended for sentient beings to understand that there is going and coming within birth and death;

it is not like the view of annihilationism. This is because it refutes the nihilistic view and the view of annihilation, [and so forth], up to the point that various karmas lead to the places of rebirth.
This means there is such karma and there is such rebirth;
by using the term "nature" (*dhātu*), it is taught that one grasps at birth and death (and so forth), up until the point of abandoning the characteristic of the self-nature of nature.
The Buddha taught that all things are like illusions; this is not because there is something established, but because he wished to bring about detachment.

In accordance with the expectations of the deluded regarding the characteristics of their evil views, [he taught]—up to and including—that the self-nature and characteristics of all phenomena are like illusions and dreams.
Fools with evil views do not know their own minds. The Tathāgata, wishing to destroy their attachment to the view of causal conditions, therefore speaks of illusions and dreams as an antidote.
It does not cause foolish people with evil views and expectations (and so forth) to perceive things as they truly are and yet formulate incorrect doctrines.
All phenomena are like illusions; thus, there is neither the perception of objects nor the view of cessation. Consequently, the characteristics of all phenomena are made to accord with reality.
Yet foolish people cling to them and claim that this teaching constitutes an incorrect doctrine.
Mahāmati, seeing all phenomena as they truly are means transcending the manifestation of one’s own mind.
Knowing that there is manifestation within the mind, the mind then revolves according to that manifestation; it has not yet reached the state of no-mind.

When the mind abides in its true state, the mind is devoid of its own [subjective] mind, and phenomena are merely phenomena themselves, like images appearing in a mirror—neither welcomed nor rejected. This is the vision of the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*).
They shall also be eliminated.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Non-arising is the absence of intrinsic nature; Intrinsic nature encompasses birth and death. One should contemplate them as being like illusions and so forth."
Regarding the non-conceptualization of signs, the verse says:
The myriad phenomena of the world manifest their own forms; The deluded, relying on others, toil in vain all day long.
Therefore it is said that the cause of illusion is suddenly extinguished by clear knowledge; it must be like a flash of lightning, a momentary light.
The teaching of "no-arising" is intended to shatter the attachments of the ignorant; one must know that the claim of "inherent existence" is merely a prescription applied according to the illness.
If one abides in the reality of mindlessness, there is not a single thing that can be conceptualized.
Chapter Thirty-one: On Being Free from Names, Phrases, and Syllables.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of names, phrases, and syllables—[and so forth]—until their entry into the meaning, phrases, and syllables.
Provisional names manifest the Path; therefore, awakening to the phrases of names is itself entry into the phrases of meaning.
One swiftly attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (and so forth), up to the ultimate certainty of intrinsic nature. This is the aggregate of names (*nāma-kāya*).
Phenomena are established by means of names; names are fixed by means of phrases; phrases manifest meanings; and meanings possess intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
Because of these intrinsic natures, they are determined and ultimate.
The "form-body" (rūpakāya)—up to this point—it is called the form-body.
The form-body is, that is to say, the letter (*vyañjana*).
Furthermore, the form-body refers to length, shortness, height, and lowness; because its own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) manifest, it is called "form."
As for the creator of characters: the long and short, the high and low, imitate their original forms; therefore it is said that "their own characteristics manifest.
This is called the body of names, phrases, and phonemes (and so forth, up to: one should practice and study them.
One who knows the bodies of names (*nāma-kāya*), phrases (*pada-kāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjana-kāya*) understands that that which is expressed lies beyond the words themselves;
the speaker is merely a means, like a fish-trap or a snare. Ordinary worldlings, however, foolishly cling to the distinctions between these bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes.
Like an elephant mired in deep mud, a verse says:
"Forms, names, chapters, and phrases are chaotic and profuse; One cannot avoid sitting by the rooster-window to investigate and study them."
Ten thousand li of rivers and lakes are like reaching the shore; what need has the traveler to guard an empty boat?
This is the thirty-second section, "Ceasing Delusion by Abandoning Characteristics.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, in future ages, those who possess wisdom (and so forth) will speak of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and cease their discourse.

"Indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) means that there is nothing to be recorded; it refers to not establishing a formal teaching. "Setting aside" (*sthāpanīya*) means to leave a matter unaddressed without answering.
The Tathāgata speaks of these as indeterminate because he fears those sentient beings will become attached to existence; thus he provides this explanation.

It is because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to the nature of the grasped and the grasper, failing to realize that all is the manifestation of one's own mind, that [the Buddha] sets them aside and does not answer.
I shall explain this for you. Those who are deluded do not realize that the general meaning of "Buddha" does not reside solely in this [etymology], yet they directly apply this title to the Buddha;
thus, they have erred.
This is not something that such ignorant people can understand (and so forth, until) they compose indeterminate treatises based on these causes.
If it is caused by the body and life, that is precisely what is meant. Therefore, it is called "with respect to causes.
Because they do not understand that all things are the manifestation of one's own mind, they cease [their activity].
The Buddha’s cessation of discourse is for this reason alone.
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, employs four modes of answering questions (and so forth), yet does not do so for those who are not yet mature.
These four modes of answering are: direct answer, answer by counter-question, analytical answer, and setting aside the question. Setting aside the question means to cease the discussion.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, all dharmas are free from being produced (up to: all dharmas are unarisen).

Because non-Buddhists maintain an indeterminate theory regarding causes, the Buddha taught that there is no arising through causes and conditions, and that neither essence nor characteristics can be apprehended.
Mahāmati, for what reason are all natures devoid of self-nature? (And so forth... It is said that all dharmas are unarisen.
Because when there is self-realization, all natures and characteristics are found to be non-apprehendable; therefore, all dharmas are unarisen.
Why is it that all dharmas cannot be brought forth (and so on, up to) cannot be taken away?
Because they have nowhere to go and nothing by which they can be grasped, they have nowhere from which they come. Since they have nowhere from which they come, what is there for them to go to?
Therefore, all dharmas are free from holding, coming, and going (and so forth), up to: all dharmas are non-extinguished.
Their intrinsic nature and characteristics are entirely non-existent; since dharmas cannot be apprehended, what is there to be extinguished?
For what reason are all phenomena impermanent? [And so forth,] therefore it is said that all phenomena are impermanent.
They are quiescent from the very beginning; how could there be impermanence? As for the nature of impermanence, it arises dependent upon the various signs of the world.
For what reason are all phenomena eternal (and so forth, up to) said to be eternal?
It is because the arising of all characteristics is, from the beginning, devoid of the nature of birth. Since they are originally without birth, that which is without birth is eternally constant.
That which is discriminated by the Perfectly Awakened One has no self-nature that can be apprehended; because it is free from verbal expression, it is said to be devoid of self-nature.
As the verse says:
The heterodox are deluded and their understanding does not penetrate; they falsely claim to bring rest to all things, confusing the ultimate truth.
If one speaks of noble wisdom, it leaves no trace; both essence and appearance are transcended, cutting off both difference and sameness.
This concludes the thirty-third chapter, on the Distinctions of the Four Fruits.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [up to] ...by means of the inexhaustible body and wealth of the realm of all dharmas, he sustains and nourishes all."
All dharmas are an inexhaustible body and wealth; this is precisely the ocean of practice in the *Avataṃsaka*.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are three kinds of *srotāpanna* (and so forth)... because they are characterized by unreal conceptualization that is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent."
The *srotāpanna* has no notion of a fool; there is neither existence nor non-existence, nor both existence and non-existence, and regarding all phenomena, they have no notion of reality.
This deluded imagination is also like that of a fool, who gives rise to deluded imagination through various attachments to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
The deluded thoughts of fools (up to and including) the deluded view of selfhood of a *srotāpanna*—this refers to the desire to eliminate the deluded thoughts of fools.
Yet, not knowing how to turn back from this, they instead follow after unreal delusions.
Regarding the "deluded view of selfhood," it is because there is the perception of a person and the absence of the perception of a self.
Mahāmati, as for the innate view of a self-body (*sahaja-satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it is because the great elements and form do not aggregate [for the *srotāpanna*].

That is to say, the *srotāpanna*, when viewing his own body and the bodies of others, sees that the characteristics of form are fundamentally empty. Although he speaks of "dispelling form," this merely serves to prolong the characteristic of birth;
this is the innate view of a self-body. As for the innate view of a self-body, it is because there is no aggregation of form and so forth.

He sees. When the stream-enterer contemplates the categories of existence and non-existence, [they] do not appear (and so on), which is called the characteristic of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
When he contemplates existence and non-existence and they all fail to appear, only then does he sever the view of a self-body, and craving does not arise.
"Mahāmati, as for the characteristic of doubt (up to): this is called the characteristic of doubt abandoned by a *srotāpanna*.
It means that because doubt regarding phenomena (*dharma*) does not arise, it is said that the characteristic of doubt is abandoned."
Mahāmati, what is the grasping of precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)? (Up to: those who seek rebirth therein do not grasp it.
This refers to foolish commoners who, observing the precepts with diligence and performing various ascetic practices, seek a place of rebirth to enjoy future happiness.
That *srotāpanna* does not grasp such characteristics; therefore, it is called "not grasping at precepts."
Except for the dedication toward one's own superior self-awakening (up to and including) the undertaking of the factors of morality;
regarding only the dedication and so forth, even though one undertakes the factors of morality, one does not truly undertake them.
This is called the severance of the characteristics of the precepts of a stream-enterer (up to: the non-severance of the view of a self-body and the various fetters).
If a stream-enterer should think, "These are the three fetters; I have abandoned these three fetters," this is called seeing two dharmas.
Consequently, he falls back into the view of a self-body, and that which was called the severance of the fetters is no longer severed.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Those who delight in women [and so forth] do not sever the craving for nirvāṇa;
rather, they attain the fruit of a srotāpanna. Because they have attained the bliss of samādhi, they are able to sever worldly craving, but they are not yet able to sever the craving for nirvāṇa."
Mahāmati asked: "What are the characteristics of a Sakṛdāgāmin? (And so on, until: the non-arising of perceived characteristics.

One thoroughly penetrates the characteristics of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) as well as the arising of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Regarding those perceived characteristics, they likewise do not arise at all."
Because they skillfully perceive the characteristics of the meditative attainments (dhyāna-gati),
[and so forth] up to causing deluded conceptualization (vikalpa) not to arise, they give rise to views of faults regarding the nature and non-nature of the characteristics of form (rūpa).
This is because they cause that conceptualization not to arise.
For the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, he skillfully manifests as an arhat who is a transformation of a Buddha’s transformation.

By means of this Buddha-transformation, he transforms and guides sentient beings; this is called "the transformation of transformations. It is the fruit of the path of the One Vehicle, manifested through the skillful means of the bodhisattva as a Buddha-transformation of a transformation. These are the three types.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Those śrāvakas who have attained the path of the single vehicle of tranquility are not others;
this refers to the arhats mentioned here, for they are indeed the path of the single vehicle, whereas those two other types are not.
Therefore, in the following passage, the two types of practice are described to clarify that the practice of the single vehicle is not like theirs."

Mahāmati, regarding the locus of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), various teachings are expounded; [this continues] up to the description of the characteristics of attaining the fruit, which is termed "attaining the fruit.

As for the practitioner of dhyāna, entering dhyāna and being entirely detached from all [objects] is called "attaining dhyāna. Because one perceives that which appears to the mind through direct cognition (*pratyakṣa*), this is called "attaining the fruit," and is designated as "attaining the fruit";
yet it is not the attainment of the fruit in reality. These two aforementioned types do not transcend the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*).
It is not the One Vehicle.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, those who wish to transcend the dhyānas, the immeasurables, and the formless realms—even up to the point where they do so because of the existence of the mind-only measure—have not yet abandoned the two former states of meditative attainment (samāpatti), namely, those involving sensation and perception. Only those who transcend the manifestation of their own minds do not [fall back].

It is likewise so; therefore, it is said that this is not the case. This is because, in order to distinguish between two types of *cittamātra*, [the text] intends to transcend the dhyānas, the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*);
from this point downward, all describes the path of the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) of quiescence.
This is merely the measure of deluded thought; if one awakens to this, there is liberation.
A verse says:
"The true mechanism of all Buddhas is not easily transmitted; it transcends all measures of form and is truly difficult to shoulder."

Having severed the three fetters and upheld the precepts with loftiness, Suddenly illuminating the fruition of non-arising already perfected, Only the Anāgāmin can perceive what lies beyond; The Arhat is capable of attaining all dhyānas.
The One Vehicle excludes this by transcending the mind-measure; Its essence merges with empty space, where no mysteries are established.
The Thirty-Fourth Section on the Two Kinds of Awakening Factors.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of awakening (up to: this is called the awakening of observation (*vicaya-bodhi*).

It is the nature of awakening itself, yet it is also the vision of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-darśana*). Thus, there is nothing to be abandoned among the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). Therefore, it is called "discernment" (*viveka*).
It cannot be apprehended apart from the four extremes.
Mahāmati, this [reality] is free from the four extremes (and so forth); one should study it by observing all phenomena.
The intrinsic nature of awakening is itself free from the four extremes; such is the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). It is only at this point that it is called "all."
Dharma. Observing all phenomena by departing from these four propositions, one first transcends the four propositions and immediately attains mastery; therefore, one should practice and study this.
Mahāmati, what is the establishment of awakening through the grasping and attachment to the characteristics of false discrimination? (And so forth... This is called false discrimination.

The cognition that establishes through mutual inclusion and attachment is the fundamental characteristic of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) upon which it relies. From this very causal characteristic, analogies are produced;
yet these are said to be all merely established upon what is unreal. To be attached to these is "establishment by existence," though fundamentally nothing exists there at all.
All established positions are false; one should further awaken to this.
This is called the two kinds of characteristics of awakening (and so forth, until) the accomplishment of these two characteristics of awakening.
Because one skillfully awakens to the two kinds, it is said that they are accomplished.
Regarding the mark of the selflessness of persons and phenomena (and so forth, until):

having attained the first stage (*bhūmi*) and entered into one hundred samādhis, through the realization of non-existence, one is then able to observe the stages of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*). Only then does one truly attain the first stage and enter into one hundred samādhis.
It is said that in the space of no more than a moment, one transcends the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*); this speaks to its swiftness.
Regarding the ten inexhaustible phrases for skillfully binding the mind: within the teachings of the *Avataṃsaka*,
these ten inexhaustible phrases mature sentient beings (and so forth, until) they attain the samādhi of self-awakened bliss.

Within the awakening of contemplation, one is free from the four extremes; reckoning others as unreal is likewise not true.
Only when there is ultimately no awakening does one become awakened; this is how one first enters the domain of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, you should skillfully understand derived form produced by the four great elements. How does a bodhisattva skillfully understand derived form produced by the four great elements?
Because there is the nature of the four great elements, they produce the form-characteristics of the four great elements.
That which is the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is that the four great elements are unarisen;
the ultimate truth is quiescent, and thus it is said to be "unarisen. Indeed, it is through the absence of the notion of arising that there is non-arising.
Those four great elements are unarisen. One should observe them in this way. (And so forth... This is called the limit of the conceptual construction manifested by the mind.
By observing those four great elements as unarisen, one is then able to realize the limits of conceptual construction;
one knows that all limits manifested by one's own mind are such that external natures are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature.
This refers to the contemplation of the three realms (up to) the universal purity that transcends the four propositions.
Within the three realms, the Bodhisattva contemplates the nature of the four great elements and derived matter as fundamentally non-existent;
thus, they transcend the four propositions and abide in universal purity without any defilement.
It is free from "self" and "what belongs to self. According to its true marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is divided into segments;

yet, having already transcended the four propositions regarding derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), it is, within its true marks and specific characteristics, the primordial state of all suchness (*tathatā*).
Therein, there is no notion of arising or ceasing; it is only in terms of conventional appearance that one speaks of "segments."
Abiding in the self-characteristic of non-arising is established.
If one abides in the true nature (*dharmatā*), one abides in non-arising; in this way, the self-characteristic is established.
Mahāmati, because consciousness delights in various traces and objective spheres, it continues on in other realms of existence.
The four great elements give rise to form, and by means of the sense-faculties and consciousnesses, one takes pleasure in all objective spheres of form.
By this, birth is continued in the other realms of existence.
Mahāmati, the four great elements such as earth and so forth, as well as the derivative forms [produced from them]—up to and including the great elements themselves—do not arise.
If one realizes that there is no intrinsic nature, then even the seeds of the four great elements have no arising; therefore, it is said that they are not conditioned by those four great elements.
[Regarding] their nature, form, and characteristics (and so forth), these are the false imaginings of the non-Buddhists and are not mine.
The verse says:
Earth, water, fire, and wind are called the four great elements; who knows they are formed by the conjunction of manifold conditions?
If one knows that the four great elements are fundamentally without self-nature, their own characteristics are suchness and do not arise at all.
Chapter Thirty-Six: The Characteristics of the Self-Nature of the Aggregates.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of the self-nature of the aggregates (up to the point where) one falsely discriminates and speaks of them as being a single space.
The four great elements are of a nature that pervades the entire Dharma-realm; yet their physical characteristics can still be pointed out and described.
As for the non-material aggregates (skandhas), they are utterly beyond numerical characteristics, like a person falsely claiming that empty space is a single entity.
Mahāmati, such aggregates (up to and including the aforementioned points) are not the domain of the noble ones (ārya).
All aggregates are devoid of characteristics, devoid of intrinsic nature, and beyond the four logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi). They exist due to delusion; once awakened, they are entirely empty.
Fools falsely cling to them, regarding them as truly existent; therefore, it is said that they are not the domain of the noble ones.
The noble Mahāmati (and so forth) [realizes that things] are free from being either different or non-different.
To the noble ones, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) appear suddenly and vanish instantly;

they are like various forms produced by illusion, or like the images in a dream or a reflection, for which one never calculates identity or difference. Thus Yongjia said: "The five aggregates are floating clouds in the void."
"Go, Mahāmati! You should eliminate the nature and characteristics of the aggregates (skandhas), which range from the sphere of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) [down to their ultimate state].
They are originally empty and quiescent, appearing solely due to false conceptualization (*parikalpita*). The purport of noble wisdom does not [accord with them]."
Falling into existence or non-existence is likewise a manifestation of one's own deluded thoughts, yet it is without any point of attachment; therefore, it is said:
"This is called the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates. You should eliminate it."
Having extinguished [them], one speaks of the Dharma of tranquility (up to and including) the purification of the view of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Although phenomena are without self, that view still persists. Only when the very nature of the view is also forgotten is there true tranquility.
And entering the Immovable Stage (up to) the universal salvation of sentient beings is likewise so.
The verse says:
The five aggregates are like floating clouds, their nature fundamentally detached; They are like dreams and shadows—do not give rise to doubt.
The view of the selflessness of phenomena remains empty and pure; like an empty-handed magician in the marketplace, [one realizes this].
Chapter Thirty-Seven: The Distinction Between the Four Kinds of Nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of nirvāṇa among the various non-Buddhists. What are these four? They are: the intrinsic nature of things (*svabhāva-svabhāva*).
Nirvana as non-existence:
this refers to failing to realize the self-nature of phenomena and thus taking that [non-realization] to be non-existence, which is itself nirvana.
This is the nirvana of the various characteristics of existence and non-existence.
This means that because all natures and characteristics are themselves non-nature, they are *nirvāṇa*.
To awaken to the fact that specific characteristics and intrinsic nature are non-nature is *nirvāṇa*.
That is to say, one first regards natures and characteristics as non-nature, and now one awakens to this; yet, in reality, one perceives this through conceptualization. This is—
Regarding nirvāṇa:
it is the cessation of the continuous flow of the individual and common characteristics of the aggregates (skandhas).
That is to say, nirvāṇa is the very cutting off of the flow of the aggregates.
These are called the four kinds of nirvāṇa of the various non-Buddhists (and so forth), up to: "the cessation of the discriminating consciousness is called nirvāṇa.
This is the nirvāṇa of the non-Buddhists; it does not transcend the seeds of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) associated with discrimination.
What the Tathāgata calls the extinction of all consciousnesses is termed nirvāṇa; it is not an entity possessing real existence.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, [and so forth]... why is it that one is free from the *manovijñāna* (mental consciousness) and not the seven consciousnesses?
Mahāmati meant: since the eight consciousnesses have been established, for what reason is it stated here only that the *manovijñāna* ceases, rather than the cessation of the seven consciousnesses?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Because of those causes and those objects of perception, the seven consciousnesses do not arise.

As for these causes and objects of perception, they initially stem from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). If the mental consciousness ceases, then the seven consciousnesses have no basis by which to arise."
The manovijñāna arises from the attachment to the segmentation of its own objects; [and so on, until: for this reason, when the manovijñāna ceases, the seven vijñānas also cease.
From the attachment to the segmentation of its own objects up to that which is produced by causes and conditions—all this is what is produced by the manovijñāna. It does not [arise] from itself.

The destruction of the marks of the body is also like this; it is that which is produced by the seven consciousnesses. Habitual tendencies (vāsanā) proliferate, nourishing and sustaining the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
The manas accompanies it, clinging to "mine" and engaging in discursive thought; thus, through the causal conditions of continuity, [the consciousnesses] arise.
As for the consciousness, if the marks of the body are not destroyed, the storehouse consciousness is the Tathāgatagarbha. The storehouse consciousness is...

Due to the conditions of objective referents, these manifest and gather within the mind, thereby giving rise to the seven consciousnesses. These seven consciousnesses are what was previously called the "manifesting consciousness" (ādarśa-vijñāna).

The mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is what was previously called the "discriminating consciousness of phenomena" (viṣaya-vikalpa-vijñāna). That which does not destroy the characteristics of the body is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).

This is precisely what was previously called the true consciousness (*amalavijñāna*). It is that which manifests as the mind; the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) discriminates, and the seven consciousnesses follow it.
When the mental consciousness is extinguished and there is nothing to grasp or rely upon, the seven consciousnesses are merely empty names and thus naturally cease.
Thus, when the mental consciousness ceases, the various forms of consciousness do not arise.
The verse says:
Deluded thoughts are tumultuous and one is unaware of them; Yet they manifest their forms within the mirror of the mind.
Thus, the seven consciousnesses are caused to grasp and give rise to objects; The various sensory realms remain within the mind for one to examine.
If the sense-faculties do not cling to their objects, like roots and stems, Then the numinous source is limpid and still—what room for doubt?
Transcendent and formless is this precious treasury; Facing it, who could fail to know that it is none other than oneself?
Chapter Thirty-Eight: The Section on the Differentiation of the Self-Nature of Discursive Thought (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the general characteristics of the differentiation of the self-nature of discursive thought.

(Omitted) That is to say, there is an object of discourse which is the self-nature known by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*); based upon that, verbal discursive thought arises. This is called "the object of discourse."

The conceptualization of objects (*vastu-vikalpa*) refers to the false discourse regarding the definitive meaning known by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*). If verbal expression arises based upon that [knowledge], it is therefore called the conceptualization of the object expressed.
This is called the delusion of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*).
Originally nothing exists, yet one falsely establishes an intrinsic nature, thinking, "This phenomenon is thus; it is not otherwise.
This is the view.
This refers to the attachment to the causes and conditions of bondage and non-bondage, as in the case of a person’s skillful means regarding whether one is bound or liberated.
That is, one clings to the cause as being able to bind, such that there is something bound— just as a person, by the power of skillful means with a rope, binds someone and then releases them again.
Mahāmati, those who are attached to dependent origination (even unto) manifesting various bodies like an illusion,
are attached to dependent origination; they give rise to attachment toward the false nature of selfhood, just as one perceives various objects based upon an illusion.
Ordinary beings perceive various diverse illusions through their false imaginings;
by means of these, they further cling to illusory appearances,
their minds bound to objective realms as conceptual cognition follows after them.

From the lines "The wisdom of non-existence and excellence / Arises as equal" onwards, up to "the existence of the self-nature of false imagination," all [sections] establish the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as being falsely posited.
The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) constitute two;
a third [truth] arises without cause.
Furthermore, the doctrine of non-arising is established in three ways:
first, the conceptualization of conventional truth; second, the severance of all such delusions within the realm of the sages;
and third, that only the sages can effect this severance.
For example, as a practitioner perceives various things within a single [reality],
and perceives a single principle within various things—
when these are ultimately not established, one transcends all false imaginings.
When one reaches the ultimate and no signs arise, then one has crossed over.
One awakens to the knowledge that these are merely *nirmāṇa* (illusory manifestations).
Since there is no distinction therein, it is only through self-awakening; thus one knows that all things perceived as distinct are but *nirmāṇa*.
Once accomplished, there is no intrinsic nature;
this refers to the intrinsic nature of accomplishment.
What is the awakening of conceptual construction?
When the nature of self-existence is realized, then all things are without intrinsic nature. How, then, could there be any cognition?
Various manifestations arise from false conceptualization; this is the pure realm of the sages.
Only the sages know that although these things appear, they are not real.
One who is free from these two types of false conceptualization—this is what constitutes the verse:
"False conceptualizations all arise due to causes and conditions; To further discuss them, there is neither difference nor identity."
It is just like repeatedly interpreting a dream while still within it; only after awakening does one realize that everything is empty.
This concludes the thirty-ninth section on the characteristics of the One Vehicle of Self-Awakening.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One... [up to] ...free from the delusions of views."
He realizes that this mind-seeing does not arise from any other cause, and he should further distance himself from it;
ascending higher and higher, he enters the stage of the Tathāgata (and so forth), until he realizes the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
The habitual tendencies of afflictions have already been severed. Furthermore, one must realize the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

If one does not realize the selflessness of phenomena, then one has not yet forgotten [attachment to] phenomena; this is like being attached to the bliss of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) or the non-substantial outflow-free realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
They have awakened to the outflow-free realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) which is non-substantiality regarding all arising afflictions (and so forth);
yet, although the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the afflictions have been severed, they have not yet awakened to the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
For the time being, they continue to savor the bliss of samādhi and the non-substantial outflow-free sphere. Regarding this, the wise person must further awaken; they should observe the One.

All things are fundamentally without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet one realizes the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*). Because the characteristics of nature have not yet been forgotten, one must remain awakened.
No vehicle is ultimate; as long as there is a mind, one falls into the three vehicles. The verse says:
Noble wisdom has no vehicle; it is called self-awakening. This means that one illuminates oneself and does not rely on others.
Craving the flavor of samādhi all constitutes an obstruction. Though the mind be untainted, it is not yet free from dust;
it will ultimately be tossed about by the winds of appearances, like a floating log drifting upon the river's edge.
The enlightened nature is vast and empty, vanishing into the void; Only then does one attain the sovereign body of the Tathāgata.
