Chapter Three: The Heart of All Buddha-Speech;
Section Forty: The Body Born of Mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "I shall now explain the characteristics of the distinctions and the commonalities of the body born of mind."
It is said: (up to) the practitioner, having realized the characteristics of advancement on the first bhūmi, attains three kinds of bodies.

Since the mind is fundamentally without marks, what can be called a "body"? It arises from the enjoyment obtained [on that stage], and because it is like a mind-born body (manomaya-kāya) without obstruction, it is called the "mind-born body. One who attains these three kinds of bodies advances beyond the first [bhūmi].
Therefore, it is said that one thoroughly understands the characteristics of advancement in the first stage (*bhūmi*).
One knows that the nature of the objects appearing as one's own mind is neither existent nor non-existent;
one knows that the nature of all that appears is not that [intrinsic] nature at all.

The body and mind undergo transformation; that is to say, one completely relinquishes the body characterized by the mind, mental factors, consciousness, the five dharmas, the three natures, and the two kinds of selflessness,
and attains the illusion-like samādhi (up to) being as swift as one's will.
The fundamental single Dharma-realm manifests hundreds of thousands of samādhis that are pure and pristine, as clear as exquisite flowers, appearing through transformation according to the mind;
therefore, it is called "swift as one's wish. The previous statement referred to what is manifested by the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); this statement refers to the illumination of all illusory marks.
It is like an illusion, a dream, the moon reflected in water, or a reflection in a mirror (and so forth), because one penetrates the dharma of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since one can penetrate that all dharmas have that [very] intrinsic nature, yet "I" have no intrinsic nature, it is called the "dharma of intrinsic nature.
If this is so, then although all dharmas appear, the dharma is eternally unstained.
What is the "body born of mental intention without effort" (manomayakāya) that arises simultaneously with its kind?
It is the universal manifestation of all phenomena within a single mind, just like images reflected in the ocean-seal. Therefore, it is called "kind."
Simultaneously arising, it is the single mind following conditions; thus, it acts without acting, like wind passing through space. Therefore, it is said to be "without activity.
The various mind-born bodies are adorned with the flowers of mastery.
The verse says:
With vast openness, the waves of all consciousnesses have been eliminated; Thus, one dwells in peace within the three types of manifestations—body, speech, and wealth.
Realizing from the outset that the source is not a substantial nature, One gradually understands them to be like illusions, and the veils of phenomena are opened.
Rising as rain and dew from the ocean of merit, Within the gate of adornment, pavilions and terraces are joined.
One must know that while there is no action, all things act together; All arise from what is spontaneously attained.
Chapter Forty-one: Departing from the Five Uninterrupted States.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught:

if a man or a woman commits the five deeds of immediate retribution (pañcānantarya-karmāṇi), [up to] these are called the five matters of immediate retribution and are also called the immediate [factors]."
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Bodhisattvas contemplate that the self-nature of all dependent origination is empty, thereby attaining the liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa*).

They contemplate that the nature of all links of existence (*bhavāṅga*) is cessation, such that not even the slightest dharma arises; they thereby attain the liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣa*). [This leads to] signlessness and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)."
Except for compassion, one attains the liberation of wishlessness; these are called the three liberations.

It is said that those who commit the five acts of immediate retribution intend to sever the seven consciousnesses of the Buddha by means of these three liberations and the perception of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), yet in reality they are unable to achieve liberation. Therefore, this is called "evil perception."
Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding the external uninterrupted [states] (up to: ...), one does not attain the dharma of uninterrupted realization (abhisamaya) in each of the three liberations.
To sever these five kinds is called "uninterrupted realization. One who severs them is one whose mind is intent upon wholesome karma.

If, within the three gates of liberation, one does not perceive the dharma of immediate realization (*abhisamaya*), then apart from this, there is the manifestation of immediate realization through the power of transformation.

Since such a manifested transformation of immediacy does not constitute ultimate severance of those [afflictions], it is called "external immediacy" (*bāhyānantarya*); it is merely a manifested transformation.
This is precisely what is meant by "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*): through wisdom and skillful means, one acts without interruption, yet has no deliberate intention toward virtuous karma;
thus, one is able to eliminate the doubts and regrets of those who have committed the five *ānantarya* sins.
This means that the spiritual power of transformation employed by Śrāvakas (and so forth, up to) does not consist in performing an act of uninterrupted [karma] in an absolute sense.

Although they manifest through spiritual power, once manifested it subsequently ceases; because it does not constitute the ultimate severance of that [affliction], it is said that there is no performance of an act of uninterrupted [karma] in an absolute sense.

One must not [perceive] the uninterrupted [stream of existence], except by awakening to the fact that it is merely the manifestation of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*). Even within this manifested continuity, there is in reality nothing at all;

it is solely the awakening to the manifestation of one's own mind. Furthermore, the nature of this manifestation of one's own mind is fundamentally no-nature. Thus, the subsequent passage states... (etc.).

Free from the false conceptions of body and wealth (and so forth, up to) liberation from the false conceptions of the continuity of other realms of existence, one manifests transformations without interval.
Originally, by means of wisdom and skillful means, one acts for the sake of sentient beings;
yet, if there remains any conception of the continuity of other realms of existence, one has not yet transcended the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*). Therefore, it is said:
These are called the five *ānantarya* [sins].

"The five kinds of *ānantarya* are most grave; When viewed with the True Eye, these karmas give rise [to rebirth]."
How can they compare to the three liberations of the mindless? There is no need for guarding or inspection; one spontaneously and perfectly becomes a Buddha. Chapter Forty-two:
On the Realization of the Selflessness of Persons and Dharmas.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "One realizes that both persons and dharmas are without self."

All say that both person and phenomena are devoid of self; have you thoroughly investigated and realized this?

The Forty-third Section on the Equality of All Buddhas.

All phenomena are of one essence.
Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and myself— through these four who are equal,
I have taught them as my sons.

In this regard, the Tathāgata merely points to "mind-only," and thereby all arising and ceasing are suddenly understood.
Regarding what is called the sequential continuity of the stages (*bhūmi*) and, furthermore, the teaching on the various activities of the three realms:
the Blessed One and all Buddhas have established the sequence of the stages and the discourse on the various activities of the three realms as an antidote for the illnesses of sentient beings.
Fools, however, fail to realize this and harbor attachments, not knowing that these were spoken by the Buddha [for a specific purpose].
Yet this has never been taught [in such a way]. The verse says:
The Ten Stages are all established as expedients for those on deviant paths; How could there be Śrāvakas upon the Grounds?
Only when the initial root is severed do they return to the Right Path; It is at the Seventh Ground that the delusion of "mind-only" finally begins to be distinguished.
On the eighth stage, one constantly maintains the samādhi of awakening; For all classes of beings, one spreads the clouds of compassion.
If one’s own mind is realized as being free from further concerns, Then the various stages of gradual progression are merely empty talk.
Chapter Sixty-three: Extinction of All Stages and Realization of Perfect Awakening.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, regarding the eighth stage of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas:
when a Śrāvaka reaches the eighth stage,
they attain the bliss of the gates of cessation-samādhi (up to the point where they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa within their own false imaginings).

This refers to those who possess the characteristics of the selflessness of persons and phenomena, as well as the view that grasps at dharmas. Because they take a mind of false conceptualization to be nirvana,
it is not the awakening of quiescent wisdom (and so forth, up to) the accomplishment of original vows, compassion, and great mercy.
The eighth bodhisattva beholds the gate of the bliss of the samādhi of quiescence and is thus able to remember and uphold their original vows;
relying on great compassion, they bring sentient beings to fulfillment.
Knowing the ten inexhaustible phrases through discernment (and so forth), up to: "Not being a cause for the Buddha-dharma, they do not arise; they arise in accordance with wisdom.
The Bodhisattva of the eighth stage has already abandoned the false conceptualizations regarding all dharmas; therein he further cultivates all Buddha-dharmas.
It is not because of this that anything else arises, yet that which does arise does not arise from false conceptualization, but arises in accordance with wisdom.
Birth. Attaining the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening (up to: whether it be correct, incorrect, or neither correct nor incorrect.
For a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage, regarding the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening, it is like a person in a dream who, facing a great body of water, desires to cross over.
Before his body had even crossed to the other side, he suddenly awoke. Having awakened, he reflected: "Is this real, or is it false?
Is it anything other than what has been seen, heard, sensed, and cognized since beginningless time—down to the mind, the mental consciousness, and the manifestations in dreams?"
What was seen previously is neither empty nor real; it is merely the熏 (xūn, perfumed) by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing since beginningless time.

It does not depart from the two characteristics of existence and non-existence. Upon reaching this point, the mind, the intellect, and the consciousness are all suddenly awakened to as being entirely like illusions and dreams, appearing in accordance with conditions. There is no thought of them departing; once awakened to, they cease and leave nothing behind.
...the nature of reality. Therefore, it is called "manifesting as a dream. To say it manifests as a dream means that once manifested, it returns to cessation;
it does not imply a notion of annihilation.
Mahāmati, in this way, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, in the eighth bodhisattva stage (and so forth), having practiced and completed [their tasks]...
The skillful means of the Buddha-dharma cause those who have not yet attained it to attain it.
In the eighth stage, the view that gives rise to conceptual construction no longer exists; what is perceived there is the further advancement from the first stage.
Up to the seventh stage, all that is practiced consists of the conceptual constructions perceived in the eighth stage.
One perceives only that all things are like illusions and skillfully abandons the mind of grasped object and grasping subject. Upon reaching this point, one might fall into doubt regarding emptiness;
therefore, one diligently cultivates the Buddha-dharma to attain what has not yet been attained—hence it is called "expedient means."

"Mahāmati, this is the nirvāṇa of the bodhisattva. (Up to: Having attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and having seen that all things are like an illusion, they nevertheless continue to perform buddha-works. This is the skillful means of nirvāṇa;

it is not the destruction or annihilation of all dharmas that is called nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is said to be 'indestructible. This is because they have skillfully transcended the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna*)."

Having attained the realization of the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), Mahāmati sequentially taught [the Dharma] concerning the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)—

even unto the state where conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is extinguished and all things are non-existent— as an analogy for Bodhisattvas who have entered the deviant paths of externalists; thus, conceptual construction is entirely extinguished.

This is the remedial dharma. If, in the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), all faculties and measures of cognition (*pramāṇa*) are extinguished, then conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is stilled and everything becomes non-existent.
This is the seventh stage of the Mind-Measure (*cittamātra-bhūmi*).
In the seventh stage, one has not yet transcended the measure of mind;
it is only upon reaching the eighth stage,
the "Stage of No-Thingness," that one finally reaches the state of no-thingness.
The third is the sixth. Regarding "Nothingness," what follows?
The verse says:
"Upon merely ascending to the eighth stage, doubt and attachment cease; The causal conditions of mind-only no longer sprout."
Having attained the skillful means of nirvāṇa for oneself, one is already free from mental consciousness;
in the sudden absence of arising, one awakens to one's own mind—who then seeks quiescence? What hindrance is there to the Buddha-dharma saving the blind masses?
If one reaches the state of the Tathāgata where nothing is realized, what was ever there to cross when dreaming of crossing water upon waking?
Chapter Sixty-Four: Departing from Permanence and Impermanence.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "If the Tathāgata, the Arhat, [and so forth] were permanent, there would be the fault of being an agent.
To say he is 'permanent' means that one forcibly establishes a nature of true permanence within the void and quiescent [reality]; therefore, it is called being an agent."
The "eternal" [proposed] by all non-Buddhists—up to and including that which is neither impermanent nor created but eternal—is flawed.
The eternity of the Tathāgata is not an eternity without cause, nor is it an eternity as a creator; it is an eternity that is both eternal and created.
Because all [conditioned things] inevitably involve transgression.
If the Tathāgata were impermanent, then upon the disintegration of the aggregates (skandhas), he would necessarily undergo cessation; yet the Tathāgata does not cease.

The characteristics of the five aggregates are, from the very beginning, devoid of intrinsic nature (svabhāva). Even if one were to insist that the aggregates disintegrate and all characteristics are annihilated, [the Tathāgata remains].
The Buddha-Tathāgata is truly not subject to annihilation.
Mahāmati, all that is produced (and so forth) would fall into the error of being entirely impermanent.
If one were to claim that impermanence is like the lack of fixed characteristics in a jar or a garment, then all phenomena would consequently fall into the category of impermanence.
The collection of requisites for omniscience would be rendered meaningless by means of skillful methods,
because they are produced. If everything that is produced were impermanent, then the entire collection of requisites for omniscience, as well as the merit and wisdom cultivated therein,
would all be empty and devoid of purpose, since they are produced and thus impermanent.
All that is performed would then be the Tathāgata (and so on, until) the fault of meaninglessness regarding the equipment for the noble wisdom of self-realization.
As previously stated, the Tathāgata is not impermanent; yet this statement implies the Tathāgata is not eternal.
If he were as eternal as space—empty and non-existent—then all the equipment for the noble wisdom of self-realization would be entirely devoid of purpose.
Mahāmati, it is like space (and so forth)... for this reason, the Tathāgata is not eternal.
Although this statement is not that he is eternal in the same manner as space, nevertheless, his nature is like that of space, being without any change or fluctuation.
Free from such faults as permanence and impermanence, whatever is taught is merely a designation for the measure of sentient beings;
how could it not fall into the extremes of permanence or impermanence?
Furthermore, Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were an unarisen permanence, (and so forth), then because of the fault of being an unarisen permanence, the Tathāgata would not be permanent.
To cling to the unarisen as being permanent is like the horns of a rabbit or a horse; they are entirely non-existent. Thus, in all directions...
[Otherwise,] all [your arguments] would be meaningless. If it were so, one would also fall into the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

This is why the Tathāgata is not eternal. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there is another matter (and so forth), namely: because the wisdom attained in uninterrupted succession is eternal, the Tathāgata is eternal.
This describes that the Tathāgata truly possesses the dharma of eternal abiding; it is not what the world refers to as "eternal" or "non-eternal.
Mahāmati, whether a Tathāgata appears in the world (and so forth), until the Buddhas and Tathāgatas abide without interruption.
The wisdom attained by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Tathāgatas is all uninterrupted; therefore, it is called "abiding.
It does not abide in empty space, nor is it something perceived by foolish commoners. (And so forth... The Tathāgata does not arise from unreal, false conceptualization.
This refers to the Tathāgata’s uninterrupted wisdom, which is definitively and eternally abiding; it does not abide in empty space, nor does it fall within the aggregates or consciousness.
It is simply the state of suchness (tathatā) when one is detached from delusive conditions.
Mahāmati, because of two dharmas—and so forth—there is the characteristic of non-dual arising.
If speech were both permanent and impermanent, there would be two dharmas; only through the dharma of non-duality can there be tranquility.
As for all dharmas being by way of the dharma of non-duality, they are without arising and without duality, because they lack intrinsic nature and characteristics.
If all things were devoid of meaning, there would be the faults of both permanence and impermanence.
If one is free from the conceptualizing intellect that distinguishes between permanence and impermanence, then according to the thesis one has established, there are various manifold meanings;
yet when observing the measure of one’s own mind, no such verbal expressions can be found.
The verse says:
Atop the summit of Laṅkā, not even a speck of dust remains; Permanence and impermanence belong to the category of causal conditions.
The non-arising of a rabbit’s horn falls into the view of nihilism; A vague, indistinct void is likewise not the truth.
If one can awaken to oneself, that alone constitutes the Way; As soon as words are uttered, it is no longer intimate.
One must reach the Tathāgata’s immediate wisdom, Transcendent and eternally abiding, surpassing all common folk.
The Extinction of Consciousness: Chapter Sixty-Five.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome... it gives rise to the ground of the abiding of ignorance and coexists with the seven consciousnesses."
Ignorance has no fundamental abiding ground; it arises only because of the existence of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Like the body of ocean waves, [it is] ultimately pure.
That which is called the *tathāgatagarbha* is free from conditioned activity, impermanence, and the theory of a self (*ātman*).
The remaining consciousnesses arise and cease.
If one falls into [the realm of] consciousness, there is arising and ceasing;
in the mental faculty (manas) and mental consciousness (manovijñāna), there are seven [consciousnesses] in every moment.
It is said that because of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), there are the seven consciousnesses.
One fails to realize that the appearances of forms are manifestations of one's own mind, and thus gives rise to feelings of suffering and pleasure; therefore, it is called "non-realization."
Failing to reach liberation from the fetters of names and signs, craving arises;
because craving arises, attachment is produced.

This is called the Tathāgatagarbha, the Ālayavijñāna. The seven consciousnesses flow on without ceasing, (and so forth) until they arise through the grasping of self-characteristics and common characteristics.
The aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) are what is called the Tathāgatagarbha, the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna); these are merely different names for it.

Because of that storehouse-consciousness, there is objective grasping (ālambana), and thus the various consciousnesses arise. However, this is not a realm known by Śrāvakas or non-Buddhists, because they do not realize it.
Regarding the two kinds of selflessness, and because they grasp at the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases,
they perceive the Tathāgatagarbha as the five dharmas and the three natures (and so forth), continuing to progress further.
That is to say, when a practitioner perceives the Tathāgatagarbha, as well as the five dharmas and the three natures,
and realizes that both persons and phenomena are entirely without self, they are then able to extinguish the successive stages and abide in the Immovable Stage (Acalā-bhūmi).
Having attained the bliss of the thirteen gates of samādhi (and so forth), they do not accept the bliss of the gates of samādhi nor the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Because they observe the Buddha-dharma through their own vows, they are able to regard and have compassion for sentient beings; thus, they do not stagnate in empty quiescence.
Therefore, regarding both the bliss of the gates of samādhi and the limit of reality, they accept neither.
Furthermore, the wisdom established through the body, intellect, and mind arises like a mental creation;
it is free from the practice of meditative concentration (samādhi).
When one is attached to the practice of samādhi, there arises the characteristic of samādhi; therefore, one should abandon it.

One should purify [the notion of] the Tathāgata and the name "ālayavijñāna" (and so forth, up to) the name "Tathāgatagarbha," for that which is called the Tathāgatagarbha is without arising or ceasing.
When there are these two designations—Tathāgatagarbha and Ālayavijñāna—then there exist these natures and characteristics, and thus arising and ceasing occur.
Therefore, one must purify them; when purified, they are non-existent.

Mahāmati, although all ordinary beings and sages alike possess birth and cessation (and so forth, up to) they do not abandon skillful means, and although it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is nameless and devoid of birth and cessation, yet these sages have never been of the same nature as wood or stone;
therefore, they all possess birth and cessation. For this reason, although practitioners possess the noble wisdom of self-realization...
The joy of the Dharma manifests before them, yet they do not abandon courageous diligence; therefore, it is said that they do not relinquish skillful means.
Mahāmati, this Tathāgata-garbha, the ālayavijñāna (and so forth), is not [the domain] of the Tathāgatas.
The Tathāgata’s treasury of non-self is suchness beyond conceptualization, primordially pure. All sounds and conditions are perceived through conceptualization;
it is merely because of being shrouded by adventitious defilements that one perceives it as impure.
The Tathāgata’s sphere of presence is like looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of one's hand.
This self-realized sphere is ever-present before him; thus, there is no longer any perception based on conceptual thought. This is because he is free from the obscuration of adventitious defilements.
"Mahāmati, regarding this meaning (and so forth), it is the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* within the Tripiṭaka that was taught for the sake of Lady Śrīmālā.
It is the sphere of wisdom accessible only to the Buddha and to other bodhisattvas of sharp intelligence who rely upon the meaning."
Knowing that the śrāvakas are attached to quiescence, one understands that the tathāgatagarbha cannot be separated from it;

knowing that the mind and thoughts involve the views of arising and ceasing, one understands that the tathāgatagarbha cannot be identified with them. Therefore, this is exclusively the sphere of wisdom of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Do not merely hear the sound and conceive the thought that you have attained contentment;
for you have not yet awakened yourself, it is therefore called "hearing-awakening.
The exceedingly profound Tathāgatagarbha dwells together with the seven consciousnesses, giving rise to the two kinds of grasping.
There are two kinds: namely, the storehouse (ālaya) and consciousness (vijñāna).
The wise remain far removed from them; the mind and what is manifested by the mind appear like reflections in a mirror, just as images appear in a mirror.

The mind is like a stage performer; the intellect is like the assistant; the five consciousnesses are its companions; and conceptualization is the audience watching the performance. The verse says: The mind is like a stage performer; The intellect is like the assistant; The five consciousnesses are its companions; Conceptualization is the audience watching the performance.
The Tathāgata’s treasure-store is but a hollow name; good and evil are all created by it.
Only when all consciousnesses are exhausted does one accord with the Way; only when the spiritual mechanism is untainted is there no birth.
If one has a mind that forms thoughts, it will be difficult to purify; even if one clings to the True Truth, one's contemplation remains unrefined.
How can it compare to that which is manifest before one, without any covering—just as if holding a *māluka* fruit in the palm of the hand?

[Regarding] the sixty-sixth section on the discrimination of the five dharmas, the three natures, the two kinds of selflessness, and the divisions of the object and the subject, the Buddha said to Mahāmati:
"The five dharmas, the three natures, and consciousness... [up to] the dwelling in the present realization of the bliss of the dharma becomes manifest."
That is to say, when a practitioner contemplates this Dharma and enters the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization,
they attain the samādhi of happiness in the present life, which constantly manifests before them and is never obscure— just as if one were looking at an āmalaka fruit held in the palm of one's hand.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Fools are attached to conventional designations of names and marks (and so forth), up to the point that they are detached from the characterized and the characteristics, as well as arising, abiding, and ceasing;
these all arise from the false imaginings of one's own mind."
They are without reality, like illusions; they rush about like wild horses; they appear according to conditions, like the moon reflected in water. All these manifest of themselves.
The nature of this self-manifestation is, from the very beginning, devoid of self and devoid of characteristics; all arise from the deluded conceptualizations of one's own mind.
In this way, they are no different from the names "elephant," "horse," "chariot," "infantry," "man," or "woman.
That is to say, one manifests their characteristics by means of such names as "elephant" and "horse.
Mahāmati, those of right wisdom (and so forth) are like travelers passing through.
Because it does not possess the characteristic of annihilation,
one abandons the two views of establishment and denial,
as well as the objects of knowledge associated with those two views of existence and non-existence, along with establishment and denial.
Names and characteristics do not arise.
It is not that names and characteristics are necessarily not established; rather, names and characteristics do not arise of their own accord.
One discerns all phenomena, such as illusions and the like, and realizes the true nature of the Dharma.
Distinguishing dharmas such as those that are like illusions and so forth, they realize for themselves the dharma-characteristics traversed by noble wisdom;
for the sake of sentient beings with various inclinations and understandings, they distinguish and teach the Dharma.
To give rise to understanding according to one's inclination is called "understanding through the mind" (*manasikāra*).
The Dharma-body is free from mental activity;
the Dharma-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and entirely transcends that which is produced by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Upon reaching this state, it is termed *tathatā* (Suchness).
This is called the Bodhisattva’s entry into that which is attained through suchness (*tathatā*).
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: “[... Are there not, for each, their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and tenets (*siddhānta*)?”

The three natures—namely, the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)—are all not separate from within the five dharmas;
therefore, it is said that they "enter into" the five dharmas.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are three kinds of self-nature... [and so forth] ...this is the nature of false imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Originally, there were no names or characteristics; all arise from false imagination.
If one relies on that which arises from false imagination... [and so forth] ...one maintains distinct and individual discriminations."
The mind is fundamentally without anything to be grasped; it is by means of discriminating various marks that there is something to be grasped. Therefore, it is called "discriminative grasping.
For this reason, dependent origination exists.
This refers to the characteristics of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the manas, the mental consciousness, and the five groups of sensory consciousness.
Because these consciousnesses possess a body and objects, they are called "bodily characteristics" (kāyalakṣaṇa).
If such characteristics are present, they are termed "vases" and so forth.
That is to say, where there is the characteristic of a jar, there is the name "jar.
Such mental states and mental factors as the jar are called false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
If one relies upon the characteristic of a jar to produce the name "jar," it is the same for the mind and its mental factors.
From beginning to end there is no awakening.
Whatever constitutes awakening is merely the conceptualization of awakening;
it is established and displayed with reference to that [object].
He shows those sentient beings that this is a characteristic unattainable by any outsider, śrāvaka, or pratyekabuddha;
since there is no longer any characteristic of a śrāvaka or outsider, it is called "the unattainable characteristic."
Correct wisdom and suchness—these constitute the characteristics of accomplishment.
The verse says:
The three natures reveal the true exposition; All enter the profound five dharmas of Laṅkā.
One must realize that names and appearances are all delusions; When utterly detached from false conceptualization, one forgets conditions.
In suchness and right wisdom, what need is there for further awakening? Only when attachment to person and phenomena is forgotten is perfection attained.
With lofty strides, one transcends beyond the three realms; From this point on, one personally plucks the lotus from within the fire.
Chapter Sixty-Seven: The Parable of the Udumbara Flower and the Ganges Sands.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Do not accept things according to how they are spoken of... (and so forth)... The Buddhas are easy to see;
they are not like the udumbara flower, which is difficult to encounter. Cease seeking through expedient means."
If one were told that [the Buddha] is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower, one would immediately give rise to despondency and timidity;
therefore, it is said that he is as easy to see as the sands of the Ganges, so as to entice them and cause them to advance.
Furthermore, at times he observes those beings to be converted (and so forth), noting that the udumbara flower has never been seen, is not being seen now, and will not be seen;

yet he speaks of the appearance of Buddhas in the world as being like the udumbara flower. This is said because it depends upon sentient beings who are capable of being converted. Therefore, it is said:
Observing those who are to be transformed, [the sūtra states]:
"The Tathāgata is seen by all in the world... (down to) like the udumbara flower.
This means that although the Tathāgata is seen by all in the world, they do not attain the realm of the noble wisdom of self-awakening; therefore, it is so said.
To say it is "like the udumbara flower" means that, Mahāmati, that which is self-established and self-validated transcends worldly expectations.
It refers to what is attained through the noble wisdom of self-realization; it is peerless in the world and surpasses all analogies. Therefore, it is said to "transcend the world."
[The interlocutor] says:
"Great Wisdom, although I have employed the analogy that the Buddhas are like the sands of the Ganges, there is no fault in this.
Comparing the Buddhas to sand is not for the sake of emphasizing their great number; the full details of this analogy are provided below in the text, as it does not convey a single meaning alone."
It is just like the Ganges River and so forth, being without any difference;

furthermore, because greed and anger have been severed, its treatment of fish, turtles, crocodiles, and other creatures is likewise without any difference. Therefore, it is said that "greed and anger have been severed."
For example, the Ganges sands are the intrinsic nature of earth (and so on, up to): likewise, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is indestructible like the Ganges sands.
Earth arises from fire, yet the foolish conceive the notion that earth is being burned; in reality, earth is not burned, nor are all embodied beings.
Both are destroyed. Ordinary beings conceive the notion that the Dharma-body is subject to destruction; however, the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is in reality indestructible.
The Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is not a physical body;
a physical body is precisely that which possesses the characteristics of a destructible form.
Just as oil cannot be obtained by pressing the sands of the Ganges (and so forth), [the Tathāgata] does not abandon the Dharma-realm, his own samādhi, or his vows;

yet, because of his great compassion, sentient beings suffer to the utmost. Consequently, he moves the Tathāgata to give rise to the fundamental vow of great compassion. Therefore, it is said that "being oppressed" is like pressing [oil from sand].
It is like pressing sand to obtain oil; it is likewise impossible to cause the Tathāgata to abandon his deep-seated aspirations and joyful resolve within the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges (and so forth)... for this reason it is said that they are "like the sands of the Ganges. The sands are a metaphor for all dharmas;
the water is a metaphor for the stream of the Dharma that flows toward nirvāṇa. Although there are a thousand transformations, they all follow toward nirvāṇa;
there is not a single dharma that does not enter nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is said that it is not that there is no water. Although...
It is said that all dharmas follow the flow toward nirvana, yet they never follow the flow of transmigration. Therefore, it is said that while they follow the flow, their nature remains constant.
The Tathāgata does not follow the flow of transmigration, for "going" (gati) signifies destruction.
Because nirvāṇa is not subject to destruction, it does not flow along with the various courses of transmigration.

Mahāmati, the original limit of birth and death is unknowable; (and so forth) it is given various names such as "the infinite" and so on, which are merely the products of one's own false conceptualization.
When the beginningless cause is extinguished, one subsequently awakens to that which is manifested by one’s own mind.

Once one awakens to the mind’s own manifestations, one is able to understand external objects and is no longer driven by false conceptualization; therefore, it is called liberation. Liberation does not mean destruction.
Although it is said to be boundless, it is not a state of total non-existence. That which is called "boundless" is likewise for the sake of sentient beings’ delusions.
These are merely different names established for the same thing.

By observing that both the internal and external are free from false conceptualization (and so forth, until) all phenomena are entirely quiescent—one observes the internal and external phenomena through the knowledge and vision of liberation, thereby becoming free from false conceptualization; there is nothing else.

There are sentient beings; it is precisely because this very deluded imagination is termed "sentient beings" that those who observe in this manner find both wisdom and its objects to be entirely quiescent.
This is because the liberated one has shattered the deluded mind of sentient beings through consciousness.
Therefore, the subsequent passage states (at length):
"Because one does not recognize that false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is a manifestation of one's own mind, conceptualization arises;

if it were recognized, it would cease. There is no concern that all conceptualizations will not cease; the only concern is that they cannot be recognized and understood. If they can be recognized and understood..."
Then false conceptualization will not arise of its own accord; this is what is called liberation.
Its nature remains constant even as it follows the stream—this is the Buddha’s verse of perfect awakening, which says:
Like the udumbara flower, it has never been seen in person; Even if the sands of the Ganges were used as metaphors, the meaning would be fully expressed.
Neither flowing nor departing, it is eternally quiescent; Without decrease and without increase, it is like the Dharma-body.
Transcending all causes and conditions, how could it be different? Though others may cause affliction and turmoil, it never gives rise to anger.
For your sake, I shall further explain the infinite measure; it is like light illuminating the atoms of all lands.
Chapter Sixty-Eight: The Distinctions of the Momentary Destruction of Characteristics.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "I only pray that you will explain for me the momentariness of all dharmas."
